Preliminary treatment consists of influent screens followed by grit removal.
An iron salts dosing station doses ferric chloride at the Emergency Basin Overflow Structure for odor control.
Following preliminary treatment, wastewater is pumped into rectangular primary clarifiers to remove floatable and settleable material.

A modified biological nutrient removal (BNR) process is employed that is designed to remove BOD and ammonia (NH3) in the same aeration basins. Each basin is divided into four sections referred to as “quads.” The first and third quads are operated under anoxic conditions, while the second and fourth quads are operated under aerobic conditions. This configuration achieves effective filament control and allows for some denitrification.
Following biological treatment, wastewater is pumped to secondary clarifiers.

Following the secondary clarifiers, the wastewater undergoes filtration. There are 16 dual media filters, 4 of which are dedicated to producing Title 22 unrestricted-use reclaimed water and 12 of which are used to produce water suitable for discharge to San Francisco Bay.
Filter backwash water is sent to a backwash equalization basin for storage, followed by flocculation and sedimentation.
Filter backwash water is sent to a backwash equalization basin for storage, followed by flocculation and sedimentation.
The settled solids from the backwash water are pumped back to the primary treatment system.
Sodium hypochlorite and ammonia are metered into the filter effluent at the head of four serpentine chlorine contact channels to produce a solution of chloramines for disinfection.
As the effluent leaves the contact channels, its chlorine residual is measured, and an appropriate amount of sodium bisulfite is added to neutralize the hypochlorite.
The channel provides additional stabilization of the treated effluent, backup aeration if low dissolved oxygen levels are detected, and a backup dechlorination system...

When at full capacity, the Center is capable of treating up to 10 MGD of the Facility’s secondary clarifier effluent using microfiltration, reverse osmosis, and ultraviolet light to produce approximately 8 MGD of high-quality recycled water.

Sludge from primary and secondary clarification operations is processed using anaerobic digesters. The process consists of dissolved air flotation (DAF) thickening, anaerobic digestion, lagoon stabilization, and dewatering using sludge drying beds.

Once dried, the biosolids are trucked to a landfill for use as alternative daily cover.

An 8-million-gallon emergency basin is available for temporary storage prior to the plant headworks, along with an additional 16 million gallons of storage after the primary clarifiers. A 10-million-gallon overflow basin is available for any overflows from the 16-million-gallon equalization basin.
A design-build project contract to construct a new headworks was awarded in June 2018. Completion is anticipated in December 2022.
Six DAFT tanks will be converted to operate as co-thickener units (thickening both primary and secondary sludges). A new primary sludge screening facility will be constructed.
Digesters 5 through 8 will be converted to Temperature-Phased Anaerobic Digestion.
